title: 315. Functions, Graphs & Transformations: Recognizing One-to-One Functions
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining condition of a one-to-one function.
questions.question: Which statement correctly defines a one-to-one function?

options.label: A
options.text: Every input has exactly one output.

options.label: B
options.text: Different inputs always produce different outputs.

questions.explanation: Every function assigns exactly one output to each input, so option A describes all functions, not specifically one-to-one functions. A function is one-to-one when no two different inputs have the same output. In symbols, if \(f(a)=f(b)\), then \(a=b\).
questions.hint: Recall the condition that starts with \(f(a)=f(b)\).

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the horizontal line test for one-to-one functions.
questions.question: A graph passes the horizontal line test if every horizontal line intersects the graph at most once. What does passing this test indicate?
questions.explanation: If some horizontal line intersected the graph more than once, then two different inputs would share the same output, so the function would not be one-to-one. Passing the horizontal line test means this never happens, so the function is one-to-one.
questions.hint: Connect multiple intersections of a horizontal line with repeated output values.

questions.concept: Identifying a One-to-One Function from Its Rule
questions.learningObjective: Determine which of two given functions is one-to-one.
questions.question: Which function is one-to-one on its domain?
questions.explanation: The function \(f(x)=3x-2\) is a nonconstant linear function, so different inputs always give different outputs; it is one-to-one. The function \(g(x)=x^2\) is not one-to-one because, for example, \(g(-1)=g(1)=1\).
questions.hint: Check whether two different inputs can produce the same output.

questions.concept: Restricting the Domain to Make a Quadratic One-to-One
questions.learningObjective: Determine which domain restriction makes \(f(x)=x^2\) one-to-one.
questions.question: Which function is one-to-one?
questions.explanation: On \([0,\infty)\), the function \(f(x)=x^2\) is strictly increasing, so different inputs give different outputs; it is one-to-one. On \((-\infty,\infty)\), it is not one-to-one because \(f(-1)=f(1)=1\).
questions.hint: Use the horizontal line test on the stated domain.

questions.learningObjective: Prove that a linear function is one-to-one by using \(f(a)=f(b)\).
questions.question: Let \(f(x)=2x+3\). If \(f(a)=f(b)\), what conclusion follows?
questions.explanation:
Assume \(f(a)=f(b)\). Then
\[
2a+3=2b+3.
\]
Subtracting \(3\) from both sides gives \(2a=2b\), and dividing by \(2\) gives \(a=b\). Therefore, \(f\) is one-to-one.
questions.hint: Start from \(f(a)=f(b)\) and simplify the equation.

questions.learningObjective: Choose a domain restriction that makes a quadratic function one-to-one.
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^2-4x+3\), which domain restriction makes \(f\) one-to-one?
questions.explanation:
Complete the square:
\[
f(x)=x^2-4x+3=(x-2)^2-1.
\]
The graph has its vertex at \(x=2\). On \([2,\infty)\), the function is strictly increasing, so it is one-to-one. On \((-\infty,\infty)\), it is not one-to-one because the parabola is symmetric about \(x=2\).
questions.hint: Find the vertex and choose one side of the axis of symmetry.

questions.concept: One-to-One from a Table of Values
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a function given by a table is one-to-one.
questions.question:
The table gives values of \(f\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\
\hline
f(x) & 7 & 5 & 7 & 3
\end{array}
\]
Is \(f\) one-to-one?

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because all four inputs are different.

questions.explanation: A function is not one-to-one if two different inputs have the same output. From the table, \(f(1)=7\) and \(f(3)=7\), so two different inputs share the same output. Therefore, \(f\) is not one-to-one.
questions.hint: Look for repeated output values in the table.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether an absolute value function is one-to-one.
questions.question: Is \(f(x)=|x|\) one-to-one on its domain?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because the graph is V-shaped.

questions.explanation:
Two different inputs, \(-1\) and \(1\), give the same output:
\[
f(-1)=|-1|=1,\qquad f(1)=|1|=1.
\]
Therefore, \(f(x)=|x|\) is not one-to-one.
questions.hint: Find two different inputs that produce the same output.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a rational function is one-to-one on its domain.
questions.question: Consider \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-2}\) on its domain \(x\ne 2\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is not one-to-one because it has a vertical asymptote.

options.label: B
options.text: It is one-to-one on its domain.

questions.explanation:
Assume \(f(a)=f(b)\) with \(a,b\ne 2\). Then
\[
\frac{1}{a-2}=\frac{1}{b-2}.
\]
Cross-multiplying gives \(b-2=a-2\), so \(a=b\). Therefore, \(f\) is one-to-one on its domain. A vertical asymptote does not by itself prevent a function from being one-to-one.
questions.hint: Set \(f(a)=f(b)\) and simplify, remembering the domain restriction.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether the composition of two one-to-one functions is one-to-one.
questions.question: If \(f\) and \(g\) are one-to-one functions, what can be concluded about \(f\circ g\), where defined?
questions.explanation:
Suppose \((f\circ g)(a)=(f\circ g)(b)\). Then
\[
f(g(a))=f(g(b)).
\]
Since \(f\) is one-to-one, this implies \(g(a)=g(b)\). Since \(g\) is one-to-one, this implies \(a=b\). Therefore, \(f\circ g\) is one-to-one.
questions.hint: Apply the definition of one-to-one twice, starting with \((f\circ g)(a)=(f\circ g)(b)\).
